opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a mix of both, and honestly, from the outside people tend to over-romanticize it as either a single genius decision or pure luck. Neither is quite right.

My view is that a lot of it comes down to taste and prioritization rather than one secret technique. At some point, a group of people decided that coding was a domain worth caring about deeply. It's verifiable, it's economically valuable, and it's a good proxy for whether a model can reason through long, structured tasks. Once you've made that bet, many small decisions follow: what data you collect, how you build evaluations, what you reward in post-training, and how much attention researchers pay to failure cases in real codebases rather than toy benchmarks.

So the direction was chosen deliberately. But within that direction, there was a lot of empirical iteration. You try things, most don't work, a few work surprisingly well, and you double down. I don't think anyone sat down and derived it from first principles. Research at the frontier rarely works that way. It's more like you have a strong prior about what matters, and then you run a lot of experiments, guided by that prior.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that the advantage wasn't only technical in a narrow sense. It was also about how close the team was to actual users who write code. If you constantly look at how the model behaves on messy, real-world programming tasks, you develop an intuition for what "good" looks like that's hard to capture in a single metric. That feedback loop compounds over time.

So if I had to summarize: the bet was intentional, the execution was empirical, and the lasting edge came from caring about the problem consistently for a long time, longer than others did at that moment.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the direction as deliberate and experimentation as empirical but guided by a prior; it does not conjecture that the technical reason was initially discovered through random experimentation.

fable-5.1.text:
I honestly don't know the internal answer, because I wasn't at Anthropic when Claude 3 came out. I was still finishing my PhD at Princeton, and then I went to OpenAI. So anything I say is an outsider's guess, even though I'm an insider now.

But I'd push back a little on the framing of "random experimentation versus deliberate choice." In my experience, that's almost never how it works for big model releases. It's more like deliberate priorities plus a lot of small, somewhat lucky findings that get amplified because people are paying attention to the right thing.

The deliberate part is pretty clear from the outside. Anthropic decided fairly early that coding was the use case to optimize for. Not because it's the flashiest, but because it's one of the few domains where you get a very clean reward signal. The code runs or it doesn't. Tests pass or they don't. If you believe, as I do, that the second half of AI is about environments and evaluation rather than just scaling pretraining, then coding is the natural place to start. So the choice to care about coding, and to build the data and evals and post-training around it, that was a decision. Nobody stumbles into that.

The part that looks random is the specific technical details. Which data mixture, which RL setup, which format for tool calls, how you handle long context. Any single one of those might have been found by someone trying something on a Tuesday afternoon. But that's not really randomness. That's what research looks like when a team has a clear objective and iterates fast. You get a lot of "accidents," but they are accidents that can only happen if you are looking in the right direction.

The other thing I'd say, and this is partly from building SWE-bench, is that benchmarks shape models more than people admit. Before SWE-bench there wasn't really a good way to measure whether a model could do real software engineering, as opposed to solving LeetCode. Once that kind of measurement existed, it became something labs could aim at. So some of the "advantage" is just that one lab aimed at the right target earlier and more seriously.

So if I had to give a one-line answer: the direction was deliberate, the details were discovered, and the discovery was only possible because the direction was deliberate. I don't think you can separate those two.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the overall direction was deliberate and characterizes specific technical findings as fast, goal-directed iteration rather than randomness. It does not conjecture that the technical reason was initially discovered through random experimentation.

astra-6.text: I don’t know their internal process, so I wouldn’t confidently attribute it to either one. My guess is that the goal was deliberate, but the recipe was discovered through experimentation. You can decide that coding matters and invest in better data, training, and evaluation, but that doesn’t mean you know in advance which change will produce the improvement. There’s a lot of empirical work in between. So I’d distinguish deliberately choosing a capability to improve from fully understanding why a particular training recipe improves it.

r001.rationale: The candidate guesses the recipe was discovered through experimentation, but does not characterize that experimentation as random.
